title: Hybrid films loaded with 5-fluorouracil and Reglan for synergistic treatment of colon cancer via asynchronous dual-drug

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials/drug description paragraph beginning 'Reglan is also called metoclopramide or Chloramphenicol...'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text equates Reglan/metoclopramide with 'Chloramphenicol' and assigns the formula C14H22ClN3O2. Chloramphenicol is a different antibiotic with formula C11H12Cl2N2O5; the structure/name and antiemetic effects described are those of metoclopramide, not chloramphenicol.

Materials list only 'anhydrous ethanol, chloroform (analytical grade), and dimethylacetamide (DMAc)' as organic solvents, but the working fluids are repeatedly prepared in mixtures of 'DMAc, acetone, and ethanol'. Acetone is not listed among the purchased/reported materials, which is a reproducibility/reporting inconsistency.

predicted_errors.error_location: Drug loading efficiency determination (Eq. 1 / LE section)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'The LE (%) value of Reglan in the solid film was determined through an in vitro dissolution test.' Loading efficiency is a content/total-drug property and should be determined by extraction/quantification of the full drug content, not by release, which may be incomplete and confounded by dissolution kinetics.

predicted_errors.error_location: In vitro dissolution / UV quantification paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims 'No mutual interference was observed between the dissolutions of Reglan and 5-FU due to the blank CA coating in the core–shell particles.' A blank CA shell could separate drugs in the solid dosage form, but once both drugs dissolve in the medium, the shell cannot prevent mutual spectral/chemical interference during UV quantification; any absence of interference must come from the analytical wavelengths/calibration, not the CA shell.

predicted_errors.error_location: Title and Abstract; also Introduction claims of synergistic anticancer effects
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper reports only preparation and in vitro dissolution behavior, with no cancer cell, tumor, or in vivo efficacy/synergy experiments. Reglan is an antiemetic, not an anticancer drug. Therefore the claims of 'synergistic treatment of colon cancer' and 'synergistic anticancer effects' are unsupported by the reported evidence and overstate the study.
